quests.questionSentence: The firm employs two hundred people, most of ___ work remotely.
quests.targetClause: whom
quests.completedSentence: The firm employs two hundred people, most of whom work remotely.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Most of whom' combines a quantifier, a preposition, and a relative pronoun; after 'of,' a person takes 'whom.' 'Most of who' is impossible, and 'most of them' would join two full sentences with only a comma, which is a comma splice.
quests.nativeTip: The clause needs a relative pronoun right after 'of.' Which one follows a preposition when the antecedent is a group of people?
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [non-defining] ➔ "whom"

quests.questionSentence: The museum owns three thousand paintings, several of ___ have never been exhibited.
quests.targetClause: which
quests.completedSentence: The museum owns three thousand paintings, several of which have never been exhibited.
quests.ruleExplanation: Paintings are things, so the pronoun after 'of' is 'which': 'several of which.' 'That' cannot follow a preposition, 'whom' is for people, and 'them' would create a comma splice.
quests.nativeTip: The antecedent is a group of things, and the pronoun follows the preposition 'of.'
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [non-defining] ➔ "which"

quests.questionSentence: The conference welcomed five hundred delegates, many of whom travelled from abroad. What does 'many of whom' refer to?
quests.targetClause: the five hundred delegates
quests.completedSentence: The conference welcomed five hundred delegates, many of whom travelled from abroad. What does 'many of whom' refer to?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Many of whom' picks out part of the group 'five hundred delegates' and adds extra information about them. The conference itself is not a group of people, so 'whom' cannot refer to it.
quests.nativeTip: 'Whom' points back to the group named just before the comma. Ask who 'many' is a portion of.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [non-defining] ➔ "the five hundred delegates"

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Verb Agreement in Quantifier Relative Clauses
quests.grammarRule: Verb Agreement in Quantifier Relative Clauses
quests.questionSentence: The library holds thousands of books, only one of which ___ available online.
quests.targetClause: is
quests.completedSentence: The library holds thousands of books, only one of which is available online.
quests.ruleExplanation: In 'one of which,' the subject of the verb is 'one,' which is singular, so 'is' is correct. 'Are' is the common trap: it agrees with 'books,' but 'books' is inside the prepositional phrase 'of which.'
quests.nativeTip: The verb follows the quantifier - 'one' - not the plural noun 'books.'
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [non-defining] ➔ "is"

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Verb Agreement in Quantifier Relative Clauses
quests.grammarRule: Verb Agreement in Quantifier Relative Clauses
quests.questionSentence: Ten students applied, three of whom ___ offered scholarships.
quests.targetClause: were
quests.completedSentence: Ten students applied, three of whom were offered scholarships.
quests.ruleExplanation: The subject is 'three,' which is plural, and the story is told in the past, so 'were' is correct. 'Was' would suit 'one of whom,' and 'is' or 'has been' would shift the tense.
quests.nativeTip: Decide which word is the subject of the verb - 'three' or 'whom' - and whether the sentence is set in the past.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [non-defining] ➔ "were"

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Verb Agreement in Quantifier Relative Clauses
quests.grammarRule: Verb Agreement in Quantifier Relative Clauses
quests.questionSentence: The team lost five players, each of whom ___ replaced within a week.
quests.targetClause: was
quests.completedSentence: The team lost five players, each of whom was replaced within a week.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Each' is grammatically singular, so the verb is 'was.' The plural noun 'players' sits inside 'of whom' and does not control the verb, so 'were' is the tempting mistake.
quests.nativeTip: 'Each' is singular, even though it refers to several players.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [non-defining] ➔ "was"

quests.questionSentence: Which sentence has the correct punctuation?
quests.targetClause: We interviewed twelve applicants, most of whom had no experience.
quests.completedSentence: Which sentence has the correct punctuation?
quests.ruleExplanation: A clause like 'most of whom had no experience' is non-defining, so it follows a comma; it has no comma after 'whom,' and it cannot use 'that.' Without the comma the clause is not properly separated, and extra commas break the phrase.
quests.nativeTip: Quantifier clauses add extra information about a group already named, so they are set off from the main clause.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [non-defining] ➔ "We interviewed twelve applicants, most of whom had no experience."

quests.questionSentence: Which sentence is ungrammatical?
quests.targetClause: The city has ten districts, all of them are safe.
quests.completedSentence: Which sentence is ungrammatical?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'All of them are safe' is a complete clause, so joining it to the first clause with only a comma is a comma splice. Using 'all of which,' adding 'and,' or splitting into two sentences all fix the problem.
quests.nativeTip: Three of these are acceptable ways to say the same thing. One joins two full clauses with nothing but a comma.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [non-defining] ➔ "The city has ten districts, all of them are safe."

quests.questionSentence: Why can't 'most of who' or 'most of that' replace 'most of whom' in 'The staff, most of whom are volunteers, run the shop'?
quests.targetClause: After a preposition, a relative pronoun for people must be 'whom,' and 'that' can never follow a preposition.
quests.completedSentence: Why can't 'most of who' or 'most of that' replace 'most of whom' in 'The staff, most of whom are volunteers, run the shop'?
quests.ruleExplanation: After a preposition, a relative pronoun for people must be 'whom'; 'who' and 'that' cannot follow a preposition at all. The rule has nothing to do with commas or with groups.
quests.nativeTip: Think about which relative pronouns may follow a preposition such as 'of.'
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [non-defining] ➔ "After a preposition, a relative pronoun for people must be 'whom,' and 'that' can never follow a preposition."

quests.questionSentence: The committee, at ___ request the report was revised, has now approved it.
quests.targetClause: whose
quests.completedSentence: The committee, at whose request the report was revised, has now approved it.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'At whose request' means 'at the committee's request,' so the possessive 'whose' is needed. This fronted-preposition-plus-'whose' pattern is common in formal writing, as in 'on whose behalf' and 'in whose honour.'
quests.nativeTip: Look at the noun after the gap - 'request.' Who or what owns that request?
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [non-defining] ➔ "whose"

quests.questionSentence: The charity, ___ behalf the funds were raised, thanked its donors.
quests.targetClause: on whose
quests.completedSentence: The charity, on whose behalf the funds were raised, thanked its donors.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'On whose behalf' = 'on the charity's behalf.' Possession requires 'whose'; 'on whom behalf' and 'on which behalf' cannot show ownership, and 'whose on' reverses the order.
quests.nativeTip: The fixed phrase is 'on behalf of' someone. Which pronoun supplies the owner of the behalf?
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [non-defining] ➔ "on whose"

quests.questionSentence: Which sentence uses the formal pattern correctly?
quests.targetClause: The manager on whose recommendation we hired her has retired.
quests.completedSentence: Which sentence uses the formal pattern correctly?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'On whose recommendation' = 'on the manager's recommendation.' 'Who's' is a contraction of 'who is,' 'whom' cannot show possession, and 'whose on' puts the preposition in the wrong place.
quests.nativeTip: Two things must be right at once: the possessive pronoun and its position after the preposition.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "The manager on whose recommendation we hired her has retired."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Phrasal Verbs and Stranded Prepositions
quests.questionSentence: Which version is standard and natural?
quests.targetClause: The colleague I look up to is retiring.
quests.completedSentence: Which version is standard and natural?
quests.ruleExplanation: Phrasal verbs like 'look up to' behave as a unit, so the preposition stays with the verb at the end of the clause. Forcing the preposition to the front separates the verb from its particle, and leaving out the particle changes the meaning entirely.
quests.nativeTip: 'Look up to' means 'admire' - the two little words belong to the verb, not to the noun.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "The colleague I look up to is retiring."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Phrasal Verbs and Stranded Prepositions
quests.questionSentence: Why is 'the plan we came up with' preferred over 'the plan up with which we came'?
quests.targetClause: 'Come up with' works as a unit, so the whole verb phrase stays together instead of being split.
quests.completedSentence: Why is 'the plan we came up with' preferred over 'the plan up with which we came'?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Come up with' is a phrasal verb: its parts work together as one unit of meaning. Fronting only part of it splits the verb apart and sounds unnatural, so speakers keep the whole phrase in place.
quests.nativeTip: Think about 'come up with' as a single chunk of meaning.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "'Come up with' works as a unit, so the whole verb phrase stays together instead of being split."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Phrasal Verbs and Stranded Prepositions
quests.questionSentence: The idea ___ she came up with saved the project.
quests.targetClause: that
quests.completedSentence: The idea that she came up with saved the project.
quests.ruleExplanation: The relative pronoun stands for 'the idea' as the object of 'came up with,' so 'that' works. 'Whom' is for people, 'in which' would add a second preposition, and 'whose' shows possession.
quests.nativeTip: 'Came up with' is a phrasal verb that stays together at the end of the clause. Which option can stand for 'the idea' as its object?
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "that"

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Preposition + which Referring to a Whole Clause
quests.grammarRule: Preposition + which Referring to a Whole Clause
quests.questionSentence: She arrived at nine, ___ time the meeting had already ended.
quests.targetClause: by which
quests.completedSentence: She arrived at nine, by which time the meeting had already ended.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'By which time' is a formal phrase meaning 'by that moment.' The preposition comes first, followed by 'which'; 'which by' reverses the order, and 'that' or 'whom' cannot follow a preposition here.
quests.nativeTip: The fixed phrase points back to the moment she arrived. Which preposition-and-pronoun pair fits?
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [non-defining] ➔ "by which"

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Preposition + which Referring to a Whole Clause
quests.grammarRule: Preposition + which Referring to a Whole Clause
quests.questionSentence: You may submit late, in ___ case you will lose ten percent of the marks.
quests.targetClause: which
quests.completedSentence: You may submit late, in which case you will lose ten percent of the marks.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'In which case' refers back to the entire situation just described. After a preposition the pronoun must be 'which'; 'that,' 'whom,' and 'what' are not possible in this fixed phrase.
quests.nativeTip: The phrase refers back to the whole idea of submitting late, not to a single noun.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [non-defining] ➔ "which"

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Preposition + which Referring to a Whole Clause
quests.grammarRule: Preposition + which Referring to a Whole Clause
quests.questionSentence: He mentioned the deadline, at which point everyone panicked. What does 'which' refer to?
quests.targetClause: The moment when he mentioned the deadline
quests.completedSentence: He mentioned the deadline, at which point everyone panicked. What does 'which' refer to?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'At which point' refers to the moment when he mentioned the deadline - the whole event, not one noun. That is why the clause is set off by a comma.
quests.nativeTip: Ask what 'point' refers to - a noun in the first clause, or a moment described by the whole clause?
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [non-defining] ➔ "The moment when he mentioned the deadline"

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Spoken vs Formal Preposition Placement
quests.questionSentence: Which version is best for a formal legal contract?
quests.targetClause: The party for whose benefit the trust was created shall receive the funds.
quests.completedSentence: Which version is best for a formal legal contract?
quests.ruleExplanation: The fronted preposition with 'whose' is the most formal way to express this relationship, and 'shall' fits contract language. The other versions are grammatical but conversational.
quests.nativeTip: Formal legal writing favors fronted prepositions and complete forms rather than conversational shortcuts.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "The party for whose benefit the trust was created shall receive the funds."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Spoken vs Formal Preposition Placement
quests.questionSentence: Which sounds most natural in a text to a friend?
quests.targetClause: The place we went to last night was packed.
quests.completedSentence: Which sounds most natural in a text to a friend?
quests.ruleExplanation: In casual messages, the preposition stays at the end and the pronoun is dropped: 'the place we went to.' The fronted version sounds like a letter, and the other two repeat or misplace the preposition.
quests.nativeTip: Texts are short and casual. Which version leaves the preposition at the end and drops the pronoun?
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "The place we went to last night was packed."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Spoken vs Formal Preposition Placement
quests.questionSentence: Which sentence mixes registers awkwardly, pairing a very formal pattern with slang?
quests.targetClause: The dude to whom I spoke was super chill.
quests.completedSentence: Which sentence mixes registers awkwardly, pairing a very formal pattern with slang?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'To whom' is a formal written pattern, but 'the dude' and 'super chill' are slang, so the sentence clashes. The other sentences are consistently casual or consistently formal.
quests.nativeTip: Look for the one where formal grammar and casual vocabulary pull in opposite directions.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "The dude to whom I spoke was super chill."

quests.questionSentence: What is the error in this sentence? 'The candidates, most of who applied online, were interviewed.'
quests.targetClause: 'Who' cannot follow the preposition 'of'; 'whom' is required.
quests.completedSentence: What is the error in this sentence? 'The candidates, most of who applied online, were interviewed.'
quests.ruleExplanation: After a preposition, a relative pronoun for people must be 'whom' - 'most of whom.' The commas are correct because the clause is non-defining.
quests.nativeTip: Check which pronoun is allowed directly after the preposition 'of.'
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [non-defining] ➔ "'Who' cannot follow the preposition 'of'; 'whom' is required."

quests.questionSentence: What is the error in this sentence? 'The house in that we lived was demolished.'
quests.targetClause: 'That' cannot follow a preposition; 'which' is required.
quests.completedSentence: What is the error in this sentence? 'The house in that we lived was demolished.'
quests.ruleExplanation: 'That' can never follow a preposition. The fronted pattern needs 'in which,' or the preposition can stay at the end: 'the house that we lived in.'
quests.nativeTip: Check which relative pronouns may directly follow a preposition.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "'That' cannot follow a preposition; 'which' is required."

quests.questionSentence: Which sentence contains two separate errors?
quests.targetClause: The colleague to who I reported, retired last year.
quests.completedSentence: Which sentence contains two separate errors?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'The colleague to who I reported, retired last year' has two errors: 'who' cannot follow a preposition, and the comma separating subject from verb is unnecessary. The defining and non-defining versions are both correct, and the sentence with only the stray comma has one error.
quests.nativeTip: Count the problems in each sentence: pronoun choice after a preposition, and comma use, are separate skills.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "The colleague to who I reported, retired last year."

quests.questionSentence: The proposal from the committee, some members of which had opposed it from the start, was finally approved. What does 'which' refer to?
quests.targetClause: the committee
quests.completedSentence: The proposal from the committee, some members of which had opposed it from the start, was finally approved. What does 'which' refer to?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Some members of which' refers to the committee, the group that has members. 'The proposal' does not have members, and 'the start' is only a time phrase.
quests.nativeTip: 'Members of' something - ask what group has members, and remember the comma.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [non-defining] ➔ "the committee"

quests.questionSentence: The study surveyed forty hospitals, half of ___ nurses worked night shifts.
quests.targetClause: whose
quests.completedSentence: The study surveyed forty hospitals, half of whose nurses worked night shifts.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Half of whose nurses' means 'half of those hospitals' nurses,' so the possessive 'whose' is needed. Quantifier plus 'of' plus 'whose' is a formal pattern found in reports and academic writing.
quests.nativeTip: The noun 'nurses' comes right after the gap. What do the nurses belong to?
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [non-defining] ➔ "whose"

quests.questionSentence: In 'The professor to whom I addressed the letter had already retired,' which words make up the relative clause?
quests.targetClause: to whom I addressed the letter
quests.completedSentence: In 'The professor to whom I addressed the letter had already retired,' which words make up the relative clause?
quests.ruleExplanation: The relative clause begins with the fronted preposition 'to' and runs through 'letter.' The main verb phrase 'had already retired' belongs to 'the professor' and falls outside the clause.
quests.nativeTip: The clause starts with the fronted preposition and ends just before the main verb.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "to whom I addressed the letter"

quests.questionSentence: Which sentence is correct and suitable for a formal report?
quests.targetClause: The staff, most of whom hold advanced degrees, were trained abroad.
quests.completedSentence: Which sentence is correct and suitable for a formal report?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Most of whom' is the correct formal pattern for people, and the clause is non-defining, so it needs a comma before it and none after 'whom.' 'Who' and 'that' cannot follow 'of,' and dropping the comma leaves the clause unseparated.
quests.nativeTip: Check the pronoun after 'of,' the comma before the clause, and the verb form.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [non-defining] ➔ "The staff, most of whom hold advanced degrees, were trained abroad."

quests.questionSentence: Which of these sentences is NOT acceptable in standard English?
quests.targetClause: The person to that I was speaking left.
quests.completedSentence: Which of these sentences is NOT acceptable in standard English?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'To that' is impossible because 'that' can never follow a preposition. The other three are acceptable: pronoun dropped, fronted 'to whom,' and stranded 'whom ... to.'
quests.nativeTip: Three of these are the same idea in different registers. One puts a forbidden pronoun after a preposition.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "The person to that I was speaking left."

quests.questionSentence: Which statement about prepositions and relative clauses is FALSE?
quests.targetClause: In a quantifier clause such as 'one of which,' the word 'that' can replace 'which.'
quests.completedSentence: Which statement about prepositions and relative clauses is FALSE?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'That' can never replace 'which' after a preposition, so it cannot appear in 'one of which.' The other statements are true: quantifier clauses are non-defining, people take 'whom' after a preposition, and 'whose' can follow one.
quests.nativeTip: Test each statement against what you know about fronted prepositions, quantifier clauses, and 'whose.'
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "In a quantifier clause such as 'one of which,' the word 'that' can replace 'which.'"
